gj-src: IRS groundspeed read off AAIB Bulletin 12/2019, fig. 3; track drawn schematically
dg-t: time since the gyro was set to 000
dg-m-still: motionless plane: nothing turns, no drift
dg-m-disc: disc turning under the sky: −15.04°/h everywhere
gc-north: north found from the horizontal part
gc-still: nothing to measure: no north, no latitude — the unit could never align
gc-disc: all vertical, everywhere: no north anywhere, and the “latitude” is 90° at every airport
gc-scale: decomposition drawn at the airport; arrows to scale with each other
lv-scale2: smaller than the altitude (R/ex, uniform scale); numbers are the real ones
rc-tas: cruise speed filed in the flight plan
rc-globe-h: Globe: shortest path on the sphere
rc-flat-h: Flat map: straight line on the disc
sc-cert: allowed for a real unit, 2 NM/h
sp-key: orange: drawn longer than the flight time allows · blue: shorter · thicker = further off
eo-rms: neighbouring lines, opposite directions, differ by
eo-inset: rms (mGal) vs the radius R put in the correction (km)
rd-true: dashed: the Earth's mean radius, 6,371 km
fx-level-alt: An aircraft flies an arc d around the Earth; the local vertical turns by the angle θ at the centre; an aircraft keeping its nose fixed follows the tangent and ends Δh higher
fx-level-7: θ: the angle at the Earth's centre
fx-eot-alt: The Earth with its axis; at latitude φ a point circles the axis on a circle of radius R cos φ; an aircraft flying east adds its speed to the ground's rotation, one flying west subtracts it
fx-eot-7: a plane: no axis to circle,
fx-eot-s: the aircraft's speed arrow is enlarged
fx-gyro-alt: The Earth's rotation Ω, parallel to its axis, splits at an airport of latitude φ into a vertical part Ω sin φ and a horizontal part Ω cos φ pointing to true north
fx-gyro-3: south of the equator Ω sin φ
fx-sch-alt: Left: a pendulum hanging from an aircraft down to the Earth's centre keeps pointing down wherever the aircraft goes. Right: on a plane, the position computed by a globe-programmed unit swings around the departure point while the true position runs away in a straight line
fx-gjt-alt: The true position and the position computed by the faulty unit on a circle, separated by the angle Δσ at the centre; the unit draws the horizon of its own position, tilted by Δσ from the true horizon
fx-gjt-2: where the unit thinks it is
fx-gjt-s: the two positions are drawn close
fx-dist-alt: Left: on the globe the distance is the arc R θ between two airports, θ being the angle at the centre. Right: on the flat disc each airport sits at a distance r from the north pole, and the distance is the straight chord between them, from r1, r2 and the difference of longitude Δλ
fx-spr-alt: Four cities can all be the same distance apart on a sphere, at the corners of a tetrahedron; on a plane they cannot: with three at the corners of a triangle, the fourth in the middle is too close to all three, and its springs are squeezed
fx-rad-alt: Two airports separated by the angle θ at the Earth's centre; the flight covers the arc R θ at the true airspeed v. Out with a tailwind at v + w and back into a headwind at v − w, the average time is longer than with no wind
sc-title: A 70 kg passenger on a bathroom scale, in the survey aircraft
sc-zero: 70.00 kg: the average of all the lines
sc-flatline: flat Earth: the same on every line
jf-sub: circles: one pair of neighbouring lines alone; dashed: the true values, 23.93 h and 6,371 km
jf-x: Ω / Ω₀, the rotation put in the correction
fx-jf-alt: Two neighbouring survey lines, one flown east with the wind, one flown west against it, and the gap d between their readings; the rotation Ω pulls the two directions apart by thousands of mGal, the radius R acts only through their difference of speed; with a steady wind only Ω cos φ + w/R would show
fx-jf-10: Ω cos φ + w/R would show
fx-jf-12: to line: Ω and R come apart
lv-sling2: grey: the rope cut, it goes straight on
fx-rope-alt: Left: a stone swung on a rope; the rope pulls it towards the hand, and if the rope is cut the stone leaves in a straight line along the tangent. Right: an airliner around the Earth; gravity plays the part of the rope, pulling towards the centre; the wings hold up almost all of the weight, and the small remainder bends the path into the circle
fx-rope-7: the wings hold up the rest
fx-world-alt: Left: a globe with the parallel at 35 degrees south, a small circle of radius R cos φ, and a meridian through both poles. Right: the flat disc centred on the North Pole; the same parallel is a large circle near the rim, of radius R times (90° − φ); the South Pole is the whole rim
fx-world-1: blue: the parallel at 35°S on each map
wd-air: measured airborne time, mean of the two directions
wd-over: faster than the aircraft can fly
wd-globe-h: Globe: great circles, the view follows the aircraft
wd-flat-h: Flat map: straight lines on the disc
bd-rms: heading error of the flat map
bd-globe: globe: headings are the great circles, nothing fitted
bd-a: the airports slide on a plane to fit the flight times (as before)
bd-key: outer ring: the great circle's heading at the first airport · inner ring: the heading the map gives it now · a radial line = the heading agrees · colours: the routes the final map gets most wrong
